name: Nomegestrol acetate
lead: Nomegestrol acetate (NOMAC) is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-norprogesterone, used in prescription contraceptive pills, menopausal hormone therapy and treatments for menstrual and other gynaecological conditions. In the appearance context, it is relevant because it combines strong progesterone-receptor activity with a weak ability to block androgen receptors; reference works suggest this antiandrogenic profile may ease androgen-driven skin problems such as acne and oily skin (seborrhea) in women who use it [1].

The chain people have in mind runs from androgen receptor blocking to less sebum stimulation to clearer skin. It is a pharmacological inference. No acne-specific trial of NOMAC has been published, and the drug is not marketed for skin [1][2].

NOMAC is sold in Europe, Australia and many other regions as Zoely (with estradiol, for contraception), Lutenyl (alone) and Naemis (with estradiol, for menopause), and it is not available in the United States or Canada [1][2]. Prolonged high-dose use has been associated with intracranial meningioma in epidemiological studies [2][15].

chain: Blocks androgen receptors weakly while activating progesterone receptors
Less androgen-driven stimulation of oil glands
Possible improvement in acne and oily skin
angle.text: Reference sources describe NOMAC as a progestin with some antiandrogenic activity, and suggest this may help acne and seborrhea in women taking it. This follows from its receptor pharmacology; no acne trial of NOMAC alone or in Zoely has been published [1].

infobox: Prescription-only; not available in US or Canada [1]

paras: Wikipedia states that NOMAC's antiandrogenic activity may help with acne, seborrhea and other androgen-dependent symptoms in women, while noting that the cited studies do not demonstrate this [1]. Estimates of its antiandrogenic potency vary widely between sources, from about 5 percent to 90 percent of that of cyproterone acetate [1]. Pharmacology reviews group NOMAC with newer progestins designed to have no androgenic, estrogenic or glucocorticoid effects and, in some cases, a partial antiandrogenic effect, as with dienogest and drospirenone [3][4][7].

NOMAC is not marketed for acne, hirsutism or hair loss, and these effects are not part of its labelled uses. Grokipedia lists acne among reported adverse effects of the drug, so skin outcomes in users are described in both directions in reference works [2].

NOMAC alone (Lutenyl, 3.75 mg and 5 mg tablets) is used for menstrual disturbances such as dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia and amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, breast pain, premenstrual syndrome and menopausal symptoms. With estradiol it is sold as the Zoely contraceptive (2.5 mg NOMAC with 1.5 mg estradiol, 24 active and 4 placebo tablets) and as Naemis for menopausal therapy [1][2]. Zoely was approved in Europe in 2011 and Australia in 2012 and is marketed in about 40 countries; Lutenyl and related products are marketed in roughly two dozen [1][2]. In France, NOMAC is no longer recommended for menopausal hormone therapy as of 2023 because of meningioma risk [1][2].

NOMAC is a potent, selective full agonist of the progesterone receptor (Ki about 3 nM). Relative receptor affinities reported on Wikipedia place it at 125 percent of progesterone's reference for the progesterone receptor and 42 percent for the androgen receptor, with no estrogen or mineralocorticoid receptor binding and weak glucocorticoid binding [1]. It suppresses ovulation through antigonadotropic action, at roughly 1.25 to 5 mg per day depending on the source; a minimal-effective-dose study in women receiving estradiol was registered in 1997 [1][2][21]. Reviews of progestin pharmacology classify it among 19-norprogesterone derivatives, which are described as more specifically progestational than the older nortestosterone derivatives [6][7][8].

Its antiandrogenic effect comes from binding the androgen receptor as an antagonist. An endocrine-marker study compared the NOMAC-estradiol pill with a levonorgestrel-ethinylestradiol pill on markers of endocrine function, the kind of measurement that informs androgenic and antiandrogenic profiles [17]. In vitro work summarised on Wikipedia reports that NOMAC may influence estrogen-converting enzymes at high concentrations but not aromatase [1].

Oral bioavailability is about 63 percent, protein binding 97.5 to 98 percent (to albumin only, not SHBG), metabolism is hepatic via CYP3A enzymes and CYP2A6, and the elimination half-life is about 50 hours (range 30 to 80), with steady state in about five days [1]. A registered pharmacokinetic study examined NOMAC, estradiol and estrone after single and multiple doses of the combined pill [11]. Liver impairment can cause accumulation, and CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers such as ketoconazole and rifampicin may alter levels [1].
NOMAC (C23H30O4, molar mass about 370.5) is the 17-alpha acetate ester of nomegestrol and the 19-demethylated analogue of megestrol acetate [1].

Wikipedia describes side effects as similar to other progestogens and usually mild: menstrual irregularities, headache, nausea, breast tenderness and sometimes weight gain, though body weight is generally unchanged [1]. Grokipedia also lists acne and irregular bleeding [2]. No serious adverse effects were reported in overdose studies; doses up to 40 times the recommended amount alone were tested [1].

Meningioma is the best-documented serious signal. Grokipedia reports that use for over a year at 3.75 to 5 mg has been associated with intracranial meningioma, with odds ratios up to 4.9 in epidemiological studies, and that MRI monitoring and contraindication in people with a meningioma apply to therapeutic use [2]. A 2024 BMJ national case-control study examined progestogens and meningioma risk [15]. A 2026 narrative review in Gynecological Endocrinology names NOMAC among progestins linked to higher risk with high-dose or prolonged exposure, with risk rising with cumulative exposure and falling after discontinuation [22]. Reports from French national data describe a dose-response relationship, and meningioma surgeries in women on these drugs reportedly fell sharply after French prescribing restrictions and MRI screening [22].

Phase 3 and registered contraceptive trials of NOMAC with estradiol include a terminated 2022 study of about 3,000 participants, and a large prospective cohort safety study of the 2.5 mg/1.5 mg pill in about 101,000 women [9][10]. Wikipedia reports the contraceptive was studied in over 4,000 women before approval [1]. Comparisons with levonorgestrel-ethinylestradiol examined endocrine markers, and haemostasis, lipid and carbohydrate metabolism [17][18].

Other trials address gynaecological uses: a randomised study of 99 women taking NOMAC-estradiol versus 98 taking dienogest for endometriosis-associated chronic pelvic pain, a phase 2b study of vaginal rings in primary dysmenorrhea, a ring dose-finding study of 666 participants, endometrial preparation before hysteroscopy, and a registered trial of postpartum relapse prevention in multiple sclerosis [12][13][14][16][20]. The Uniplant one-year subdermal implant, developed in Brazil, reportedly had a one-year failure rate of 0.94 percent in trials but was never commercialized [1][19].
No acne, skin or hair trial of NOMAC was found.

Nomegestrol was patented in 1975, and NOMAC (code TX-066) was first described in 1983 by Theramex Laboratories of Monaco [1]. It was introduced in Europe in 1986 as Lutenyl and, with estradiol, as Naemis [1]. The combined contraceptive Zoely was approved in Europe in 2011, the year the US FDA rejected the US application, and in Australia in 2012 [1][2]. Several development projects, including an oral NOMAC for breast cancer, a vaginal ring, and a continuous oestradiol-NOMAC menopausal product, were not completed [1].

Brand names include Lutenyl, Naemis and Zoely [1]. NOMAC is prescription-only and available in much of Europe, Latin America and Asia-Pacific but not in the United States or Canada [1]. No community discussion of it as a distinct topic was found.

card.summary: A mildly antiandrogenic progestin in European pills; any acne benefit is suggested by its pharmacology, with no acne trial found.
card.note: Prescription-only; not available in the US or Canada; meningioma risk reported with prolonged therapeutic doses.

quick.overview:
Nomegestrol acetate is a prescription progestin used with estradiol in the Zoely contraceptive pill and alone for some gynaecological conditions. It is sold in Europe and Australia but not the US.

It has mild antiandrogenic activity, so acne improvement is suggested in reference works, but no acne trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It selectively activates the progesterone receptor to suppress ovulation and has weak androgen receptor blocking activity.
quick.risks: Reported effects are typically mild: irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. Prolonged use at therapeutic doses has been associated with meningioma in epidemiological studies. Prescription-only.
